08 — Overview

How interruption and steering work. Read this before you write code.

Two clocks, one conversation

A run is not a function call. It takes seconds, sometimes minutes, and a person is sitting in front of it. Two things become possible:

  • stop it;
  • say something while it is going.

Both need the same thing: a boundary where a new event can enter without corrupting the conversation. That boundary is the end of a turn.

Abort: the text already arrived

The important property is not "the program stops". It is that stopping does not erase what the user already read.

A streaming client accumulates text as it arrives. When the request is cancelled, the read fails part-way. Most implementations return an empty message with an error, and the caller prints the error. That loses the half-sentence the user was looking at, and it makes "I interrupted it" indistinguishable from "it crashed".

So the parser returns both:

return Message{Role: RoleAssistant, Content: content.String()}, usage,
	fmt.Errorf("read stream: %w", err)

and the loop keeps it:

if err != nil {
	if msg.Content != "" {
		history = append(history, msg)
	}
	...
}

Three consequences, and all three are graded:

BehaviourWithout it
partial text printedthe user sees an error and loses the answer
exit code 130a script cannot tell interrupted from failed
the turn persistedthe next run repeats work the user already saw

Exit 130 is the shell convention for a process stopped by SIGINT (128 + 2). It is not a detail: if agent -p ...; then ... should be able to reason about it.

Steering: a boundary, not a merge

The tempting implementation is to append what the user typed to the prompt. That is wrong in a way that looks fine on a short run: the model answers a prompt the user did not type, and the reply addresses a question that was already being answered.

The correct place is the end of the turn:

  request 1:  system, user("add a flag")
  reply 1:    "I added the flag."
  steer:      "also check the tests"        ← typed during reply 1
  request 2:  system, user, assistant, user("also check the tests")

Two properties follow, and both are graded:

  1. It is a new message, not an edit. The first request must not contain the

steering text at all.

  1. It keeps the run alive. If the model said it was done and the user then says

something, the run must continue. Stopping would ignore the person.

  done condition:  no tool calls  AND  nothing steered

That and is the whole design. Without it, a steered message after a finished answer is accepted, recorded, and ignored.

A queue needs a lock and a clear

Steering arrives on a goroutine reading stdin, and is consumed on the loop's goroutine. Two rules make that safe:

  • Drain takes and clears under a lock. A queue that is read but not cleared

replays the same instruction every turn.

  • Drain never blocks. A hook that waits for input turns the loop into a program

that waits for a human, which is the opposite of the feature.

func (s *StdinSteering) Drain() []Message {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	if len(s.queue) == 0 {
		return nil
	}
	out := s.queue
	s.queue = nil
	return out
}

Why this chapter edits the loop

Every previous chapter added files. This one changes loop.go, and that is deliberate: steering is a state transition inside the loop, not a policy around it. The budget could be a provider decorator because it only rewrites a request. Steering changes the history the loop owns, so it belongs there.

The rule is not "never touch the loop". It is "touch the loop only for loop state". This is loop state.

What this chapter does not do

  • No interactive UI. Steering comes from stdin as lines, which is enough to

prove the mechanism without building a terminal application.

  • No queue persistence. An undelivered steered message dies with the process.
  • No graceful process-group teardown. A cancelled tool's grandchildren are

still the known limitation from chapter 03.

Where the real implementations go further

Concernpicrush
Steering messagesgetSteeringMessages in the loopinternal/agent/coordinator.go
AbortAbortSignal through every layercontext plus a cancel channel
Queue drain pointsafter the assistant turn, one-at-a-time or allqueued run ids

pi distinguishes steering from follow-up messages: steering enters during a run, follow-ups only after it ends. This chapter has one queue, which is the honest minimum for two graded claims.

Self-check

  1. What must survive an interrupt, and what does the exit code 130 tell a script?

(Abort: the text already arrived)

  1. Where does a steered message enter, and what is wrong with merging it into the

prompt? (Steering: a boundary, not a merge)

  1. State the done condition of the loop in one line. *(Steering: a boundary, not a

merge)*

  1. Why must Drain clear the queue, and why must it not block?

(A queue needs a lock and a clear)
